q: What personal data does the Act protect?
a: Any information that can identify you — your name, ID number, phone number, location, email, even an online identifier like an IP address. If it can be traced back to you, it's "personal data" under the Data Protection Act, 2019.

q: What are my rights as a data subject?
a: Under Section 26, you have the right to be informed when your data is collected, to access what an organisation holds on you, to object to processing, to have inaccurate data corrected, and to have false or misleading data deleted. Other sections add further rights — to restrict processing, to data portability, and not to be subject to a purely automated decision that significantly affects you.

q: Can a company use my data for anything once I've given it to them?
a: No. Section 25 requires personal data to be collected for an explicit, specified, legitimate purpose, and not used for anything incompatible with that purpose. Using your data for an unrelated purpose without a fresh lawful basis is itself a breach of the Act.

q: Do I have to consent before a company can use my data?
a: Not always — consent is only one of eight lawful bases under Section 30. Others include performing a contract with you, complying with a legal obligation, or the company's legitimate interests, provided those don't override your rights. Where consent IS the basis relied on, Section 32 puts the burden of proving it on the organisation, and you can withdraw it at any time.

q: What happens if a company loses my data or gets hacked?
a: Under Section 43, if the breach creates a real risk of harm to you, the organisation must notify the ODPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, and tell you directly in writing within a reasonable time — unless they genuinely cannot identify you. If they miss the 72-hour window, they must explain why.

q: Can my employer monitor my calls, emails or location?
a: Employers can process employee data where necessary for the employment relationship, but the same principles apply — it must be proportionate, employees should generally be informed, and undisclosed monitoring that goes beyond what's necessary can itself breach the Act.

q: My data was used to train an AI model without asking me — is that legal?
a: It depends on the lawful basis relied on and whether the use is compatible with the purpose your data was originally collected for. This is one of the fastest-moving areas of Kenyan data protection right now — see our AI governance work in the Knowledge Centre.

q: How do I get a company to delete my data?
a: Write to the organisation (or its Data Protection Officer, if it has one) invoking your rights under Sections 26 and 40. They're expected to act without undue delay. If they don't respond, or refuse without a lawful reason, you can complain to the ODPC.

q: What is a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
a: A risk assessment an organisation must carry out under Section 31 before starting any processing likely to create a high risk to people's rights — before launching a new surveillance system or a large customer database, for example. If the assessment shows a genuinely high risk, the organisation must consult the ODPC before going ahead.

Only under the conditions in Sections 48–50 — broadly, the organisation must show the ODPC it has adequate safeguards in the receiving country, or the transfer must fit a specific necessity ground such as performing a contract with you. Transferring sensitive personal data abroad additionally requires your consent.

q: Is my medical or health information given extra protection?
a: Yes. Health data is "sensitive personal data" under Part V of the Act, and can generally only be processed by, or under the responsibility of, a healthcare provider, or someone under a professional duty of confidentiality.

q: How long can a company keep my data?
a: Only as long as reasonably necessary for the purpose it was collected for, unless retention is required by law, consented to, or for a recognised purpose like historical or statistical research (Section 39). After that, it must be deleted, anonymised or pseudonymised.

q: What can I do if the ODPC doesn't act on my complaint?
a: The Act requires complaints to be investigated and concluded within 90 days (Section 56). Where the ODPC has genuinely failed to act, our Case Digest includes an example of the High Court compelling the regulator to respond through an order of mandamus.

q: Do I need a lawyer to file an ODPC complaint?
a: You can file directly — but how a complaint is framed materially affects the outcome, and several matters in our Case Digest turned on exactly that. If your matter is contested, involves significant harm, or the other side has counsel, it's worth getting advice before you file.

q: Can a company use my photo or image without asking?
a: Generally, no — using someone's image, especially for commercial purposes like advertising, without consent can itself be unlawful processing of personal data. See Kipchirchir v Hornbill Rongai Limited in our Case Digest, where an advocate's image used without consent resulted in a KES 1.5 million damages award.

Race, health status, ethnic origin, religion or conscience, genetic and biometric data, property details, marital and family details, and sexual orientation are all "sensitive personal data" under the Act, and are processed only on narrower grounds than ordinary personal data.
